say: Heavy weights to grow, light ones to tone.
In twenty-one studies, with every set taken to the last possible rep, light and heavy loads built similar size.
The WHO minimum: strength work at least twice a week.
Across fifteen studies, more weekly sets per muscle went with more growth, in the range tested.
With weekly sets kept equal, it made no real difference, across twenty-five studies.
It's a preference, not a secret.
In a small trial, one sleepless night cut muscle protein building by eighteen percent the next day.
Extra protein helps a little, up to about one point six grams per kilo a day.
In a small study, frail ninety-year-olds grew their thigh muscle nine percent in eight weeks.
The WHO adds balance and strength training, to prevent falls.

schoenfeld2017load: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgić J, Ogborn D, Krieger JW. Strength and hypertrophy adaptations between low- vs. high-load resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Strength Cond Res 2017;31(12):3508 to 3523 (OpenAlex abstract rebuild): all sets "performed to momentary muscular failure"; "the protocol lasted for a minimum of 6 weeks"; "21 studies"; 1RM strength gains greater "in favor of high-load training, whereas no significant differences were found for isometric strength"; "The findings indicate that maximal strength benefits are obtained from the use of heavy loads while muscle hypertrophy can be equally achieved across a spectrum of loading ranges."
whoeurope: WHO Regional Office for Europe, fact sheet "Everyday actions for better health: WHO recommendations" (page dated 17 July 2025): adults (listed under 18 to 64 years): "Include muscle-strengthening activities at least 2 times per week."; older adults (listed under 65+ years): "Same as adults, with added focus on functional balance and strength training to prevent falls."
schoenfeld2016vol: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger J. Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Sports Sci 35(11):1073 to 1082 (online 19 July 2016; OpenAlex abstract rebuild): "The final analysis comprised 34 treatment groups from 15 studies." "The findings indicate a graded dose-response relationship whereby increases in RT volume produce greater gains in muscle hypertrophy." Three bands "(<5, 5" to "9 and 10+ per muscle)" showed only a trend "(P = 0.074)".
schoenfeld2018freq: Schoenfeld BJ, Grgić J, Krieger J. How many times per week should a muscle be trained to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the effects of resistance training frequency. J Sports Sci 37(11):1286 to 1295 (online 17 December 2018; OpenAlex abstract rebuild): "a total of 25 studies were deemed to meet inclusion criteria." "Results showed no significant difference between higher and lower frequency on a volume-equated basis." "In conclusion, there is strong evidence that resistance training frequency does not significantly or meaningfully impact muscle hypertrophy when volume is equated." "Thus, for a given training volume, individuals can choose" (middle of the sentence garbled in the rebuild) "based on personal preference."
lamon2021: Lamon S, Morabito A, Arentson-Lantz E, Knowles O, Vincent GE, Condo D, Alexander SE, Garnham A, Paddon-Jones D, Aisbett B. The effect of acute sleep deprivation on skeletal muscle protein synthesis and the hormonal environment. Physiol Rep 2021;9(1):e14660 (OpenAlex abstract rebuild): "Healthy young adults (N = 13; seven male, six female) were subjected to one night of total sleep deprivation (DEP) or normal sleep (CON) in a randomized cross-over design." "Postprandial skeletal muscle protein fractional synthesis rate (FSR) was assessed between 13:00 and 15:00" "Acute sleep deprivation reduced skeletal muscle protein synthesis by 18% (CON: 0.072 ± 0.015% vs. DEP: 0.059 ± 0.014%·h-1, p = .040)."
morton2018: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar S, Schoenfeld BJ, Henselmans M, Helms ER, Aragon AA, Devries MC, Banfield L, Krieger JW, Phillips SM. A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults. Br J Sports Med 52(6):376 to 384 (online 11 July 2017; OpenAlex abstract rebuild): "Data from 49 studies with 1863 participants showed that dietary protein significantly (all p<0.05) increased changes (means (95% CI)) in:" "one-repetition-maximum (2.49 kg (0.64, 4.33)), FFM (0.30 kg (0.09, 0.52))" "1.62 g/kg/day resulted in no further RET-induced gains in FFM"
fiatarone1990: Fiatarone MA, et al. High-intensity strength training in nonagenarians: effects on skeletal muscle. JAMA 1990;263(22):3029 to 3034 (OpenAlex abstract rebuild): "Ten frail, institutionalized volunteers aged 90 ± 1 years undertook 8 weeks of high-intensity resistance training." "Strength gains averaged 174%±31% (mean ± SEM) in the 9 subjects who completed training." "Midthigh muscle area increased 9.0%±4.5%." No control group described in the abstract.
peterson2010: Peterson MD, Sen A, Gordon PM. Influence of resistance exercise on lean body mass in aging adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc 43(2):249 to 258 (online 11 June 2010; OpenAlex abstract rebuild): "Randomized controlled trials and randomized or nonrandomized studies among adults ≥ 50 yr were included." "data from 49 studies, representing a total of 1328 participants, were pooled using random-effect models." "The weighted pooled estimate of mean change in LBM was 1.1 kg (95% confidence interval = 0.9" to "1.2 kg)." Older age: less increase "(β = -0.03, P = 0.01)". "RE is effective for eliciting gains in LBM among older adults"
